85.title: Augustine (354–430)
85.hook: a brilliant, restless young man hears a child singing take and read and opens the Bible
85.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Augustine on 28 August, the day after his mother Saint Monica, and many read his Confessions as a classic of prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, intercession: why Catholics ask Mary, and friends, to pray for them. Your line was pray for us. Did you ask someone? Day eighty-five. A new week: the saints, one by one.

Milan, the emperor's city. A young professor of rhetoric, paid to make speeches and to teach others to make them. He has a career, admirers, a partner of many years, a son. And he is miserable. He's been searching for years: philosophy, the Manichees, ambition, pleasure. His mother, Monica, has wept and prayed for him through all of it. He knows, by now, that he wants to follow Christ. He just can't make himself do it. In the Confessions he owns up to a prayer from his younger years, and it's painfully honest. In Pusey's translation: "Give me chastity and continency, only not yet." Today: the saint who said not yet.
screen: `BRILLIANT, SUCCESSFUL, MISERABLE.` → `A MOTHER WHO PRAYED.` → `ONLY NOT YET.`

segments.voice: Augustine grew up in North Africa, in what's now Algeria. His book the Confessions tells his life as one long prayer to God, and its turning point is in a garden in Milan. He's sitting under a fig tree, weeping, sick of himself. Then from a house nearby he hears a child's voice, singing something like a game, over and over. In Pusey's translation: "Take up and read; Take up and read." He can't think of any children's game with those words. So he takes it as a sign, goes back to where he'd left a book of Paul's letters, opens it, and reads the first thing his eyes fall on. It's from Romans: not in partying and drunkenness, not in sleeping around, not in fighting and envy, "But put ye on the Lord Jesus Christ." He says a light flooded his heart and the doubt just went. He was baptized the next Easter by Ambrose, the bishop of Milan. Monica saw it before she died. He went home to North Africa and served as a bishop there for the rest of his life, writing constantly. The Church names him a Doctor of the Church. And the line people carry from him sits on the very first page of the Confessions: "Thou madest us for Thyself, and our heart is restless, until it repose in Thee." In Augustine's telling, the restlessness isn't only a flaw. It points somewhere.
screen: `A GARDEN IN MILAN.` · `A CHILD SINGS: TAKE UP AND READ.` · `PUT YE ON THE LORD JESUS CHRIST.` · `A RESTLESSNESS THAT POINTS SOMEWHERE.` · then, large: `OUR HEART IS RESTLESS, UNTIL IT REPOSE IN THEE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: take up and read. If there's a Bible near you, or one on your phone, open it anywhere and read one verse. Just one. If there isn't, bring to mind any line of Scripture you already know. Then settle and breathe, and let it sit. Don't analyze it. Notice if anything in it catches. This isn't fortune-telling. It's just letting a word find you. If you pray, you can ask what it's saying to you today. The bell holds the time.
Augustine. The restless, brilliant North African who heard a child sing take up and read, and became a bishop and a Doctor of the Church. Today's word.
Your line: our heart is restless. Today, when you feel restless, don't just scroll it away. Ask what it's looking for. Day eighty-five.

86.title: Patrick (c. 5th century)
86.hook: kidnapped from Britain as a boy, enslaved in Ireland, he returns freely to the people who held him
86.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Patrick on 17 March, a holy day in Ireland, and many pray the prayer known as Saint Patrick's Breastplate, though it was probably written later.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Augustine, the restless genius who heard a child sing take up and read. Your line was our heart is restless. What was your restlessness looking for? Day eighty-six.

March seventeenth: green everything, parades, a river dyed green in Chicago. The Saint Patrick on the greeting cards comes with snakes, a shamrock and an Irish accent. Here's the surprise: he wasn't Irish. And we don't have to guess about him, because he left us two short pieces of writing in his own words. The longer one he called his confession. It opens with him calling himself a sinner, very unlearned, the least of all the faithful. Not a legend. A man. Today: what Patrick himself says happened.
screen: `GREEN RIVERS AND GREETING CARDS.` → `HE WASN'T IRISH.` → `HIS OWN WORDS.`

segments.voice: Patrick grew up in Roman Britain. His father was a deacon, his grandfather a priest. And by his own account, he didn't take any of it seriously. Then, when he was about sixteen, raiders from Ireland attacked his family's estate and carried him off with thousands of others. He was sold as a slave and spent six years herding animals on a cold hillside. And that's where his faith woke up. He writes that he prayed a hundred times in a day, and almost as many at night, in snow and frost and rain. One night he heard a voice in his sleep telling him a ship was ready. He walked, he says, about two hundred miles to the coast, talked his way onto a ship, and got home. Free. Safe. Family. And then the part that's hard to believe. He had a dream. A man came to him with letters, and he heard the voices of the Irish, calling him to come back and walk among them again. So he went back. Not as a slave this time, but as a bishop, to the island where he'd been owned, to the people who had held him. He spent the rest of his life there, baptizing thousands, facing threats and even arrest. And the famous bits? The snakes: there were no snakes in Ireland to drive out, and he never mentions any. The shamrock explaining the Trinity: a lovely story, but it only shows up in writing many centuries later. The true story needs no help.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: pray for someone who hurt you. Settle and breathe. Patrick went back to the people who enslaved him. You don't have to do anything that big, and you don't have to go back to anyone who isn't safe. Just bring to mind one person who hurt you. Notice what happens in your body. Breathe. Then, if you can, wish them one good thing. If you pray, you can pray for them by name. If no good wish comes today, let that be all right, and try another day. The bell holds the time.
Patrick. A British boy enslaved in Ireland, who escaped, and then freely went back to the people who had held him. Today's word.
Your line: he went back. Today, return to one place or person you've avoided, if it's safe to, even just with a message. Day eighty-six.

87.title: Benedict and Scholastica (6th century)
87.hook: twin brother and sister; she prays for a storm so he'll stay and talk
87.howItsDone: Benedictine monks and nuns live by the Rule of Saint Benedict, praying the hours together and working in between; Catholics keep Scholastica's feast on 10 February and Benedict's on 11 July.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Patrick, the boy enslaved in Ireland who freely went back. Your line was he went back. Day eighty-seven. Today, a brother and a sister, and the best argument between siblings in the history of the saints.

Italy, the five hundreds. Benedict runs a monastery on a mountain called Monte Cassino. His sister Scholastica leads a community of women not far away. Tradition says they were twins. Once a year they meet at a little house halfway between, and spend the day talking about God. One year, it gets dark, and she asks him to stay the night so they can keep talking. He says no. Absolutely not. His own rule says a monk sleeps in the monastery. So Scholastica folds her hands on the table, puts her head down on them, and prays. And out of a clear evening sky comes a storm so violent that nobody can set foot outside. Today: two saints and one thunderstorm.
screen: `A BROTHER AND A SISTER.` → `STAY THE NIGHT? NO.` → `A STORM FROM A CLEAR SKY.`

segments.voice: The story comes from Pope Gregory the Great, who wrote Benedict's life about fifty years after he died. Benedict, stuck, says something like: God forgive you, sister, what have you done? And she answers: I asked you, and you wouldn't listen. So I asked my God, and he listened. Now go, if you can. They talk all night. Three days later, Scholastica dies, and Benedict buries her in the tomb he'd prepared for himself. Gregory adds a line people still quote: she could do more, because she loved more. Here's why it matters. Benedict wrote one of the most important books in Western history: a short Rule for monks. It opens with one word, listen, and it arranges a whole day around prayer, work and reading, in balance, so no one is crushed and no one is idle. Monks and nuns still live by it, fifteen centuries later. For a thousand years, Benedictine monasteries kept books, farms, schools and hospitality alive across Europe. The Rule says every guest should be welcomed as Christ himself. The motto people give it is pray and work, in Latin ora et labora. Those exact words aren't in the Rule. They're a later summary, but a good one. And the storm is the perfect footnote. Even the man who wrote the rule had to learn from his sister that love can outrank a schedule.
screen: `I ASKED MY GOD, AND HE LISTENED.` · `SHE COULD DO MORE: SHE LOVED MORE.` · `A RULE THAT BEGINS: LISTEN.` · `ORA ET LABORA.` · then, large: `LOVE CAN OUTRANK A SCHEDULE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep an unhurried conversation. Settle and breathe. Think of someone you always talk to in a rush: between meetings, in the car, half-looking at a screen. Picture sitting down with them with nowhere else to be, like Scholastica at that table. What would you ask? What would you finally have time to hear? Let that picture be real for a minute. If you pray, you can pray for that person, and for time. The bell holds the time.
listen. The first word of Benedict's Rule for monks, which balanced prayer, work and reading across the whole day.
Your line: pray and work. Today, put a small pause of prayer or quiet between two pieces of work, and keep one conversation unhurried. Day eighty-seven.

88.title: Clare of Assisi (1194–1253)
88.hook: she follows Francis into poverty and leads her sisters for forty years
88.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Clare on 11 August, and the Poor Clares, her sisters, live enclosed lives of prayer and poverty in monasteries worldwide.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Benedict and Scholastica: his Rule opens with listen, and a storm that made a brother stay. Your line was pray and work. Did you keep one conversation unhurried? Day eighty-eight.

Palm Sunday night, in the hill town of Assisi. A young woman from a noble family waits until the house is asleep. Her family has marriage plans for her. She has other plans. She slips out a side door, through the dark streets, down the hill, to a tiny chapel in the woods where a man named Francis and his barefoot brothers are waiting with torches. There, she takes off her fine clothes, puts on a rough tunic, and Francis cuts off her long hair. By morning her family is furious. They come to drag her home. Today: the girl who wouldn't go back.
screen: `PALM SUNDAY NIGHT, ASSISI.` → `OUT THE SIDE DOOR.` → `FRANCIS CUTS HER HAIR.`

segments.voice: Her name was Clare, from the Latin for bright, clear. Her relatives found her in a convent chapel and tried to pull her away. She held on to the altar cloth and showed them her cropped head. They gave up. Soon her younger sister Agnes ran away to join her too. Francis gave them a home at San Damiano, a small, run-down church just outside town, and there Clare led a community of women, the Poor Ladies, for the rest of her life. Here's the thing to understand. Other convents owned land, so the sisters were secure. Clare refused. She fought popes, politely and for years, for what she called the privilege of poverty: the right to own nothing at all, and to trust God and the kindness of the town for bread. Two days before she died, the pope finally approved the rule she had written for her sisters herself. And she wasn't grim about any of it. The people who knew her described her as joyful. Poor and glad. Once, the story goes, soldiers came over the walls of San Damiano. Clare, sick in bed, had the Blessed Sacrament carried to the door and prayed before it, and the soldiers left. Near the end, too ill to get to Mass, she said she could see and hear it on her wall. That's why, in 1958, the Church made her the patron saint of television. Her sisters, the Poor Clares, still pray in monasteries all over the world.
screen: `CLARA: BRIGHT, CLEAR.` · `SAN DAMIANO, FOR LIFE.` · `THE PRIVILEGE OF POVERTY.` · `PATRON SAINT OF TELEVISION.` · then, large: `POOR AND GLAD.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: simplify one thing. Settle and breathe. Think of one thing in your life that's gotten too full: a closet, a calendar, a phone's home screen, a habit of buying. Picture it with less. Not empty, just lighter. Notice how that feels in your chest. Clare wasn't trying to be miserable. She was trying to be free. Pick the one thing you'll simplify today. If you pray, you can ask for the gladness she had. The bell holds the time.
clara. Latin for bright or clear, Clare's own name, who gave up everything to own nothing at all.
Your line: poor and glad. Today, give away, clear out or cancel one thing, and notice whether you feel lighter. Day eighty-eight.

89.title: Catherine of Siena (1347–1380)
89.hook: a dyer's daughter who cared for plague victims and wrote hard letters to popes
89.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Catherine of Siena on 29 April; she is a patron of Italy and of Europe, and her letters and her book, the Dialogue, are still read as guides to prayer.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Clare, clara, bright and clear, who fought for the right to own nothing. Your line was poor and glad. What did you clear out, and did you feel lighter? Day eighty-nine.

Siena, in Italy. A wool dyer's house, smelling of vats and wet cloth, crowded with children and never, ever quiet. Catherine is one of the youngest. Her parents want her married. She wants to give her whole life to God. So, as a teenager, she cuts off her hair, and her furious family makes her do the housework like a servant. She doesn't fight them. She just decides, she says later, to build a room inside herself where she can always be with God, whatever her hands are doing. Today: the dyer's daughter who ended up telling popes what to do.
screen: `A CROWDED DYER'S HOUSE.` → `SHE CUTS OFF HER HAIR.` → `A ROOM INSIDE HERSELF.`

segments.voice: Catherine joined a group of Dominican laywomen who wore the habit but lived at home. For three years she hardly left her little room, praying. Then, she said, she was sent out. When plague swept Siena, she nursed the sick others were afraid to touch. She walked with a young man condemned to death all the way to the executioner's block, and held his head. And then she started writing letters. She couldn't write well herself for most of her life, so she dictated them, sometimes several at once, to friends taking turns. Hundreds survive, written to soldiers, queens, friends and popes. Here's the context. For decades, the popes had lived not in Rome but in Avignon, in France. Catherine thought the pope belonged in Rome, with his flock. So she wrote to Pope Gregory the Eleventh, bluntly and lovingly. She called him, in Italian, something like sweet daddy, and then told him to be a man, stop being afraid, and come back. She even traveled to Avignon to say it to his face. And he did go back to Rome. She died a few years later, still young. In 1970 Pope Paul the Sixth named her a Doctor of the Church. And today's line? People often quote her as saying: be who God meant you to be and you will set the world on fire. That's a modern paraphrase. What she actually wrote to a friend was closer to: if you are what you should be, you'll set all of Italy on fire. Either way, the point is hers.
screen: `NURSING THE SICK, HOLDING A HEAD.` · `HUNDREDS OF LETTERS.` · `COME BACK TO ROME.` · `A DOCTOR OF THE CHURCH.` · then, large: `IF YOU ARE WHAT YOU SHOULD BE.`

segments.voice: Here's the practice: say one true thing kindly. Settle and breathe. Think of something you've been needing to say to someone: a hard truth, a boundary, a worry about them. Catherine was blunt, but she wrapped her bluntness in love. Picture saying it, simply, with warmth, no sarcasm, no speech. Choose the first sentence. Let it be kind and true at once. And remember her room inside: if you pray, you can go there now, and ask for courage. The bell holds the time.
sweet daddy. What Catherine of Siena called the pope in her letters, before telling him, lovingly, to come home to Rome.
Your line: be who god meant. Today, send or say the hard, kind sentence you've been putting off. Day eighty-nine.

90.title: Joan of Arc (1412–1431)
90.hook: a farm girl who led armies, was burned at nineteen, and was declared innocent 25 years later
90.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saint Joan of Arc on 30 May; she is one of the patron saints of France, and many ask her prayers for courage.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Catherine of Siena, who called the pope sweet daddy, and told him, lovingly, to come home. Your line was be who god meant. Did you say the one true thing? Day ninety.

France, 1429, deep in a war with England that has dragged on for generations. A peasant girl of about seventeen from a village in the east, who can't read or write, walks into the court of the uncrowned king and tells him God has sent her to lift the siege of Orléans and see him crowned. Nobody in that hall is expecting her, and plenty of them doubt her. She has no title and no training. Within a few months, the siege is lifted and the king is crowned. Today: Joan of Arc.
screen: `FRANCE, AT WAR.` → `A FARM GIRL AT COURT.` → `ORLÉANS, 1429.`

segments.voice: Joan said that from about the age of thirteen she heard voices, which she identified as Saint Michael, Saint Catherine and Saint Margaret. They told her to go and help the king. She cut her hair, put on armor, and rode at the front of the army carrying a banner. She said at her trial that she loved her banner far more than her sword, and carried it so she wouldn't have to kill anyone. The siege of Orléans broke. That summer, the king was crowned at Reims with Joan standing beside him. Then it fell apart. A year later she was captured and sold to the English, who put her on trial before a church court run by a bishop on their side. She had no lawyer. For months, learned men tried to trap her. One trap became famous: are you in God's grace? Say yes, and she's proud. Say no, and she's condemned herself. A nineteen-year-old with no schooling answered, in effect: if I am not, may God put me there, and if I am, may God keep me there. By later accounts, her questioners were stunned. They burned her anyway, in Rouen, in 1431. She asked for a cross to be held up where she could see it. Twenty-five years later, with the pope's approval, a new church trial declared the first one unjust and cleared her name. In 1920 she was declared a saint. So the same Church that condemned her, through a bishop, later admitted it was wrong and honored her. Today's line, I am not afraid, comes from a saying people hang on her; that exact sentence isn't in the trial records. What the records do hold is a teenager answering learned men for months without backing down.

Joan wept at her trial, and kept answering. Picture one small step you could take. If you pray, you can ask for her courage. The bell holds the time.
Orléans. The besieged city Joan of Arc helped free, months before the king's crowning and her own capture.

91.title: Thomas More (1478–1535)
91.hook: Henry VIII's chancellor, beheaded for conscience, joking on the scaffold
91.carry: the king's good servant, god's first
91.howItsDone: Catholics keep the feast of Saints Thomas More and John Fisher on June 22; many lawyers attend a yearly 'Red Mass', and More is invoked as patron of statesmen and politicians.

segments.voice: Yesterday, Joan of Arc: the girl who freed Orléans, led armies, and was burned at nineteen. Your line was I am not afraid. Where did you stand by what you knew was right? Day ninety-one.

London, July 1535. A man climbs a scaffold on Tower Hill. He's been in the Tower for over a year, and he's thin and gray. The steps are shaky, so he turns to the officer beside him and says, more or less: help me up, and as for coming down, I'll manage that myself. He was famous for jokes like that. Not long ago this man was Lord Chancellor to King Henry the Eighth. He wrote Utopia. He was a friend of the king. And he's about to die because of one thing he would not say. Today, Thomas More.
screen: `TOWER HILL, JULY 1535.` → `A JOKE ON THE SCAFFOLD.` → `ONE THING HE WOULD NOT SAY.`

segments.voice: Thomas More was a London lawyer, a father of four, with a house full of books, children, animals and arguments. He gave his daughters the same serious education as a son, which was rare then. He loved the law, and he loved his king. Then Henry wanted his marriage to Catherine of Aragon ended, and the Pope wouldn't do it. So Henry broke with Rome and had himself declared head of the Church in England. More resigned as chancellor and went quiet. But in 1534 every leading subject was told to swear an oath that went with the king's new marriage and against the Pope's authority. More refused. And here's the clever, careful part: he refused silently. He never said why. More believed that under English law, silence could not be treated as treason, so he held his tongue and trusted the law he'd served all his life. It didn't save him. At his trial, a witness named Richard Rich testified to words More swore he never said. Only then, condemned, did More speak his mind about the Church. On the scaffold, the story goes, he said he died the king's good servant, but God's first. He didn't hate the king. He just knew the order. It's honest to add: as chancellor, More pursued Protestants hard, and some were burned in those years. Catholics honor him as a martyr of conscience, and historians still argue over that record. The Church canonized him in 1935, and Pope John Paul the Second named him patron of politicians.

segments.voice: Here's the practice: keep one quiet promise. Settle, and breathe. Think of a promise you've made that nobody is checking. To call someone. To stop saying a certain thing. To be honest about something small. Pick one. You don't have to tell anyone, the way More didn't explain himself. Just hold it and decide to keep it. If you pray, you can ask Thomas More to pray for you, the way Catholics ask the saints. The bell holds the time.
